item.title: Google DeepMind Formally Verifies Signal Protocol Implementation Using AlphaProof Code AI Agents
item.description:
Google DeepMind Formally Verifies Signal Protocol Implementation Using AlphaProof Code AI Agents

Google DeepMind researchers have used AlphaProof Code, an agentic framework, to mathematically prove key security properties of the actual code underlying the Signal protocol. This technology protects billions of private conversations in applications such as Signal and Google Messages. This work represents the first time the implementation of a widely deployed protocol has been formally verified at this depth by any method, with or without AI.

🔍 Overview

Formal verification is the process of mathematically proving that code runs correctly without flaws, offering the highest standard of security assurance. While typically labor-intensive, this process was applied to the core cryptographic code of Signal to verify its privacy guarantees against potential flaws that could expose millions of users. The agents proved that the compiled code fulfills security properties—such as maintaining message protection before and after a device is temporarily compromised—down to the exact code running on devices.

🧩 How it works

AlphaProof Code is a multi-LLM agentic framework that organizes work similarly to a research team, where human experts collaborate with AI agents to achieve formal verification.

  • Specification: Researchers worked with a mix of models to translate Signal’s security goals into formal mathematical specifications, with human experts reviewing every specification.
  • Proof Generation: AI agents powered by Gemini Carbon performed the proofs, generating over six million lines of Lean, a computer language used for the mathematical verification of code.
  • Auditing and Review: The agents audited the proofs and highlighted only one percent of the codebase for human review, allowing experts to focus their judgment where it was most needed.
  • Bug Detection: To confirm accuracy, researchers reintroduced two previously fixed bugs into an isolated version of Signal’s code. AlphaProof Code successfully produced machine-checked proofs that the buggy versions were insecure.

⚙️ Key details

Attribute Detail
Framework AlphaProof Code (multi-LLM agentic framework)
Model Engine Gemini Carbon
Language Lean (mathematical proof language)
Verification Time Four weeks (historically takes expert teams years)
Scope Production code for the Signal protocol
Lines of Lean Generated Over six million

🚀 Availability

The formal verification artifacts from this research are being open-sourced for community use. This project was developed by a team including Swarat Chaudhuri, Andrew Ferraiuolo, Anton Kovsharov, Tej Chajed, Sam Schlesinger, Karn Seth, Jonathan Katz, Charles Sutton, and Pushmeet Kohli.

💡 Why it matters

Cryptographic protocols are the foundation of digital communication for banking, browsing, and messaging. While most verification stops at the design level, verifying the actual implementation helps defend against modern, agent-driven cyber threats. This achievement demonstrates how AI can bring elite security assurance to critical infrastructure, including medical device firmware and power grid software, by creating software with mathematical proof that its protections work.

#DeepMind #AlphaProof #Cybersecurity #FormalVerification #AIagents

Source: Formal Verification of Signal’s Protocol with Gemini

item.title: Proof‑Driven Development introduced with PDD Kit and Verus for Rust
item.description:
Proof‑Driven Development introduced with PDD Kit and Verus for Rust

Proof‑Driven Development (PDD) arrives as a new software‑development paradigm supported by PDD Kit. The toolkit helps teams turn their intent into formal specifications, automatically proves the generated code for every input, and falls back to tests when a proof cannot reach.

🔍 Overview

  • Coding agents can now generate whole features that span tens of thousands or hundreds of thousands of lines of code.
  • Traditional line‑by‑line review does not scale to this output, and tests often only check what the agent built, not what was originally requested.
  • A plan is meant to be the contract between a developer and an agent, but the agent is not forced to obey it, leading to hidden gaps that surface only as bug reports or edge‑case failures.

🧩 How it works

  1. Intent → Formal Spec – PDD Kit works with you to express the parts of your intent that can be formalized as a specification in Verus.
  2. Proof Generation – The kit automatically generates a mathematical proof that the agent’s code satisfies the formal spec for every possible input.
  3. Fallback to Tests – Anything the proof cannot reach (e.g., third‑party cryptography libraries, UI code) is turned into informal specifications and covered by high‑quality unit, end‑to‑end, terminal‑automation, and browser‑automation tests.
  4. TCB Sign‑off – The boundary between proved code and tested code is the Trusted Computing Base (TCB). PDD Kit makes this line explicit and asks the developer to sign off on each piece.
  5. Collaboration Environment – The workflow runs inside GitHub Next’s Chopin, a real‑time, multiplayer planning environment where teams and agents can co‑author a shared document.

⚙️ Key details

  • PDD Kit – the toolkit that drives the Proof‑Driven Development process.
  • Verus – the verifier used today; a proof language for Rust co‑developed by Microsoft Research, Carnegie Mellon University, VMware Research, ETH Zurich, MPI‑SWS, UNSW Sydney, the University of Texas at Austin, the University of Michigan, the University of British Columbia, the University of Wisconsin–Madison, and the Weizmann Institute of Science.
  • Chopin – the planning interface that lets a team and agents iterate on the plan and proposed tests before handing off implementation.
  • Formal verification – a mathematical proof that code satisfies its specification for every input, providing stronger assurance than testing alone.
  • Evidence vs. Proof – a passing test is labeled as evidence; only a verifier‑checked proof guarantees correctness for all inputs.
  • Real‑world case – inside Chopin, PDD Kit was used to formally verify the login logic of Pet Store, a Rust storefront. Verus hardened the code, uncovered existing bugs, and proved the absence of login bugs with respect to the specification.

💡 Why it matters

  • Proofs cover the entire input space, catching bugs that a test suite—no matter how large—might miss.
  • By making the TCB explicit, teams understand exactly which pieces rely on trust and can review them separately.
  • The approach scales to agent‑generated code where traditional code review is infeasible.
  • It bridges the gap between the plan (the contract) and the shipped code, reducing the hidden mismatch that typically appears only after deployment.

📊 Components at a glance

Component Role
PDD Kit Turns intent into formal specs, generates proofs and tests
Verus Verifier that checks Rust code against formal specs
Chopin (GitHub Next) Real‑time, multiplayer planning environment for teams and agents

#ProofDrivenDevelopment #FormalVerification #AIcodingAgents #Rust

Source: Formally verifying agent-written full-stack web apps with PDD Kit - Microsoft Research

item.title: Introduction of MAGS Unified Multi-Agent Framework for Verified Program Generation
item.description:
Introduction of MAGS Unified Multi-Agent Framework for Verified Program Generation

Researchers have introduced MAGS, a unified multi-agent framework designed to generate executable programs with formal safety guarantees.

🧩 How it works

MAGS utilizes Dafny as a verification-aware intermediate representation to allow safety properties to be mechanically checked. The process involves the following steps:

  • Formalizing and freezing human-audited APIs and safety requirements.
  • Translating generated code into Dafny.
  • Repairing violations using feedback from a verifier.
  • Compiling verified programs back into executable code.

⚙️ Key details

MAGS was evaluated across 220 examples, achieving a 100% success rate in producing programs with non-trivial safety guarantees against frozen specifications. The evaluation included:

Task Type Number of Examples
CUDA kernels 100
Terminal scripts 100
Robotic-arm tasks 20

#MAGS #Dafny #FormalVerification #AIagents #SoftwareSafety

Source: MAGS: Multi-agent Auto-formalization Guarantees Safety for Agentic Outputs Source: AutoData: Agentic Search for Pre-training Data Selection
